position: both — but *big* meaning older (*my big sister*) only before a noun
takes: *on* + noun or *-ing* (informal: very enthusiastic about); *of* + person in *That's big of you*
contrast: Double the *g*: *bigger*, *biggest*, never *biger*. *Big* and *large* both mean большой, but *large* is more formal and goes with *amount*, *number*, *quantity* and sizes; only *big* means important (*a big decision*), older (*my big brother*) or popular (*big in Japan*), so *a large mistake* and *my large brother* are wrong. In *think big* and *talk big*, *big* is an adverb.

senses.gloss: Large in size, number or amount.
examples: They live in a *big* house outside Denver.
Texas is *bigger* than France.
That was the *biggest* pizza I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Important, serious or significant.
examples: Getting married is a *big* decision.
It's no *big* deal, so don't worry about it.
The *biggest* problem is money.

senses.gloss: Older or grown-up; used mainly with children and about brothers and sisters.
examples: My *big* sister taught me to drive.
You're a *big* boy now, so you can tie your own shoes.

senses.gloss: Very popular or successful.
examples: The band is still *big* in Japan.
Podcasts got really *big* during the pandemic.
He was one of the *biggest* stars of the '80s.

senses.gloss: Doing something a lot or with great enthusiasm; informal *big on*: very enthusiastic about.
examples: I'm a *big* fan of her early work.
He's never been a *big* eater.
My dad is *big* on camping.

senses.gloss: Generous or kind; often said with irony.
examples: It was *big* of him to admit he was wrong.
You're lending me a dollar? That's really *big* of you.

position: both — but *fat* about money (*a fat bonus*) and in *fat chance* only before a noun
contrast: Double the *t*: *fatter*, *fattest*. Calling a person *fat* is rude in American English; say *overweight*, *heavy* or *big*. For food with a lot of fat, use *fatty* or *rich* (*fatty meat*), not *fat meat*; *low-fat* and *fat-free* use the noun *fat* (жир). *Fat chance* means the opposite of what it seems: almost no chance.

senses.gloss: Having a lot of extra flesh on the body.
examples: The cat got *fat* after we moved to the city.
He was a *fat* kid, but he lost the weight in high school.
Our dog is *fatter* than the neighbor's.

senses.gloss: Thick, full or swollen.
examples: She pulled a *fat* envelope out of her bag.
He came home from the game with a *fat* lip.
It's the *fattest* book on the reading list.

senses.gloss: Of money: large.
examples: She signed a *fat* contract with a big law firm.
The company lost money, but the CEO still got a *fat* bonus.

senses.gloss: Informal and ironic: very little or none, in *fat chance* and *a fat lot of good*.
examples: Will he pay you back? *Fat* chance.
A *fat* lot of good that did us.

contrast: Double the *t*: *hotter*, *hottest*. Russian splits heat in two, жаркий for weather and rooms and горячий for things you touch; English uses *hot* for both. *I'm hot* = мне жарко, never *It's hot to me*. Weather that is only pleasant is *warm* (тепло); *hot* is too much. *Hot* food can mean spicy (острый), so say *spicy* when you mean pepper. *Hot* about a person is informal and means sexy, so be careful with it.

senses.gloss: Of weather, a place or a time: having a high temperature.
examples: It was a *hot* day in July.
Phoenix is one of the *hottest* cities in the country.
Why is it so *hot* in here?

senses.gloss: Of food, drink or an object: at a high temperature.
examples: Careful, the pan is *hot*.
I'd love a cup of *hot* coffee.
The water for tea should be *hotter* than that.

senses.gloss: Of a person: feeling too warm.
examples: I'm *hot*. Can we turn on the AC?
The kids were *hot* and tired after the hike.

senses.gloss: Spicy, with a burning taste.
examples: This salsa is really *hot*.
Do you want the mild sauce or the *hot* one?
Their wings are the *hottest* in town.

senses.gloss: Very popular, successful or in demand at the moment.
examples: It's the *hottest* restaurant in Brooklyn right now.
Immigration was a *hot* topic in the debate.
The Celtics are *hot* and have won eight straight games.

senses.gloss: Full of strong feeling, especially anger or excitement.
examples: The meeting turned into a *hot* argument.
He has a *hot* temper.

senses.gloss: Informal: sexually attractive.
examples: All her friends thought the new lifeguard was *hot*.
He's even *hotter* in person.

senses.gloss: Informal: stolen.
examples: He didn't know the watch was *hot*.
The police traced the *hot* TVs to a warehouse.

senses.gloss: Of an electrical wire: carrying current.
examples: Don't touch the black wire; it's *hot*.
Connect the *hot* wire to the brass screw.

senses.gloss: In guessing and hiding games: very close to the answer.
examples: You're getting *hotter*. It's somewhere near the couch.
Now you're *hot*! Look under the pillow.

takes: *about* + noun or *-ing*; *for* + person (sad on their behalf); *to*-infinitive (*sad to hear*); *that*-clause
contrast: Double the *d*: *sadder*, *saddest*. The same word describes the person and the cause: *I'm sad* (мне грустно) and *a sad movie* (грустный фильм), with no *-ing/-ed* pair to choose from. Russian мне грустно is *I'm sad* or *I feel sad*, never *It's sad to me*. *A sad excuse for* is informal and scornful: a very bad example of something.

senses.gloss: Feeling unhappy.
examples: She was *sad* to leave her friends behind.
Don't look so *sad*. It's only a week.
I've never felt *sadder* than on the day we sold the farm.

senses.gloss: Making people feel unhappy.
examples: It's a *sad* movie, so bring tissues.
The *saddest* part is that nobody called her.

senses.gloss: Unfortunate and deserving regret or blame.
examples: It's *sad* that so many kids go to school hungry.
The old theater is in a *sad* state.

senses.gloss: Informal: poor, pathetic or embarrassing.
examples: That's a *sad* excuse for a burger.
I spent Saturday night alone with my laptop. How *sad* is that?

contrast: Double the *n*: *thinner*, *thinnest*. Russian splits what English calls *thin*: тонкий (a slice, a wall), худой (a person), жидкий (soup, hair). About people, *thin* is neutral or slightly negative, *slim* is a compliment, and *skinny* is often negative. Russian тонкий about taste, humor or a difference is *subtle*, not *thin*: *a subtle joke*.

senses.gloss: Having a small distance between the two sides or surfaces.
examples: Cut the cucumber into *thin* slices.
The walls in this apartment are really *thin*.
The ice is *thinner* near the middle of the lake.

senses.gloss: Of a person or animal: having little fat on the body.
examples: He was tall and *thin*, with glasses.
She looked *thinner* after being sick.

senses.gloss: Of a liquid: watery, not thick.
examples: The soup was too *thin* and bland.
Add water until the paint is *thin* enough to spray.

senses.gloss: Not dense; with few people, hairs or things, or with little oxygen in the air.
examples: His hair is getting *thin* on top.
The crowd was *thin* for a Friday night.
The air is *thinner* up in the mountains.

senses.gloss: Weak and not convincing.
examples: The evidence against him is pretty *thin*.
That's a *thin* excuse.

senses.gloss: Of a voice or sound: high and weak.
examples: She answered in a *thin*, shaky voice.
The cheap speakers sounded *thin*.

contrast: Double the *t*: *wetter*, *wettest*. Russian влажный is usually not *wet*: say *damp* for clothes or walls, *humid* for air, *moist* for cake or skin; *wet* means really covered with water (мокрый). *Wet* is also a verb whose past form is usually *wet* (*The baby wet the bed*).

senses.gloss: Covered with or full of water or another liquid.
examples: Take off those *wet* shoes before you come in.
My hair is still *wet*.
The grass was *wetter* than it looked.

senses.gloss: Of paint, ink or cement: not yet dry.
examples: *Wet* paint. Do not touch.
Don't walk there; the concrete is still *wet*.

senses.gloss: Of weather or a season: rainy.
examples: It's been a cold, *wet* spring.
November is usually the *wettest* month here.

senses.gloss: US: of a town or county: allowing the sale of alcohol.
examples: The county voted to go *wet* in 2012.
You have to drive to the next *wet* county to buy beer.

position: both — but *fit for* and *fit to* (suitable) mostly after a verb
contrast: Double the *t*: *fitter*, *fittest* (*survival of the fittest*). Russian подходить по размеру is the verb *fit* (*The jacket fits*; past *fit* in American English), not the adjective, so *The jacket is fit* is wrong. The adjective means healthy, or good enough in quality (*fit to eat*). In everyday American speech *in shape* is often more natural: *I'm out of shape*. British slang *fit* (attractive) is not American.

senses.gloss: Healthy and strong, especially from exercise.
examples: My grandmother is really *fit* for her age.
He's a *fit*, athletic guy who runs every morning.
I'm *fitter* now than I was in college.

senses.gloss: Good enough or suitable for a purpose.
examples: The water isn't *fit* to drink.
After the flood, the house was no longer *fit* for people to live in.
He'd had three beers and wasn't *fit* to drive.

senses.gloss: Right or proper, in *see fit*: to decide that something is right.
examples: Spend the money however you see *fit*.
The judge can give whatever sentence she sees *fit*.

position: both — but *flat* meaning fixed (*a flat fee*) or complete (*a flat refusal*) only before a noun, and after the note name in *B flat*
contrast: Double the *t*: *flatter*, *flattest*, spelled like the verb *flatter* (льстить). *A flat* meaning an apartment is British; Americans say *apartment*, and in American speech *a flat* is usually a flat tire. An empty battery is *dead* in American English, not *flat*. In *lie flat*, *fall flat* and *in ten seconds flat*, *flat* is an adverb.

senses.gloss: Level and smooth, without hills, bumps or holes.
examples: Kansas is famously *flat*.
Lay the map on a *flat* surface.
The land gets *flatter* as you drive east.

senses.gloss: Wide but not deep or high; of shoes: without a raised heel.
examples: She keeps her jewelry in a *flat* wooden box.
Wear *flat* shoes, because we'll be walking a lot.

senses.gloss: Of a tire or ball: without enough air in it.
examples: We got a *flat* tire on the way to the airport.
The basketball is *flat* again.

senses.gloss: Of a drink: no longer fizzy.
examples: The soda went *flat* because someone left the cap off.
This beer tastes *flat*.

senses.gloss: Of paint or a surface finish: not shiny.
examples: We used *flat* paint on the ceiling.
A *flat* finish hides small dents in the wall better than a glossy one.

senses.gloss: Dull, without feeling, energy or interest.
examples: He spoke in a *flat*, tired voice.
The second half of the movie felt *flat*.

senses.gloss: Of sales, prices or growth: not rising.
examples: Sales were *flat* in the third quarter.
Wages have stayed *flat* for years.

senses.gloss: Of a price or charge: the same in every case.
examples: The lawyer charges a *flat* fee of $500.
They offer a *flat* rate for shipping.

senses.gloss: Complete and firm, with no discussion.
examples: Her answer was a *flat* no.
The senator issued a *flat* denial.

senses.gloss: In music: lower than the correct note; after a note name, a half step lower.
examples: The piece is in B *flat*.
The violins sounded a little *flat*.

contrast: Double the *m*: *slimmer*, *slimmest*. About people, *slim* is a compliment, *thin* is neutral and *skinny* often is not. *A slim chance* and *slim hopes* are very small ones (мало шансов) and have nothing to do with shape. *Slim down* is a phrasal verb (худеть).

senses.gloss: Of a person: thin in an attractive way.
examples: She's tall and *slim*, with short dark hair.
He looks *slimmer* since he started cycling.

senses.gloss: Of an object: thin or narrow.
examples: The new phone is *slimmer* and lighter.
He published a *slim* book of poems.
These jeans have a *slim* fit.

senses.gloss: Of a chance, amount or difference: very small.
examples: There's only a *slim* chance of finding survivors.
She won by the *slimmest* of margins.
Pickings are *slim* this late in the season.

position: both — but *grim* meaning determined (*grim determination*) only before a noun
contrast: Double the *m*: *grimmer*, *grimmest*. *Grim* is not simply dark: about a face it means serious and stern (суровый), about news or a situation very bad and worrying (мрачный, удручающий). A room with little light is *dark* or *dim*, not *grim*; a *grim* room is depressing to be in. *The Grim Reaper* is the figure of Death.

senses.gloss: Of a face or expression: very serious and stern.
examples: The doctor came out with a *grim* look on her face.
His expression grew *grimmer* as he read the letter.

senses.gloss: Very bad, worrying or depressing.
examples: The economic news is *grim*.
Things look *grim* for the home team.
It was the *grimmest* winter anyone could remember.

senses.gloss: Of a place: unpleasant and depressing to be in.
examples: They spent the night in a *grim* motel off the highway.
The waiting room was gray and *grim*.

senses.gloss: Determined and not giving up, even when things are hard.
examples: She held on with *grim* determination.
The workers fought a *grim* battle to keep the factory open.

position: both — but *dim* in *take a dim view* only before a noun
contrast: Double the *m*: *dimmer*, *dimmest*. *A dimmer* is also a noun, a switch that makes lights less bright (диммер). *Take a dim view of* means disapprove of (относиться неодобрительно), not see badly. Calling a person *dim* is informal and unkind. *Dim* is also a verb: *dim the lights*.

senses.gloss: Not bright; with little light.
examples: The bar was *dim* and smoky.
She read by the *dim* light of a candle.
The lights get *dimmer* when the AC turns on.

senses.gloss: Hard to see, hear or remember clearly.
examples: I have only a *dim* memory of my grandfather.
We saw a *dim* shape moving in the fog.

senses.gloss: Of chances or prospects: not hopeful.
examples: Prospects for a deal look *dim*.
His chances of winning grow *dimmer* every day.

senses.gloss: Informal: not intelligent.
examples: He's nice, but a little *dim*.
He's not *dim*, just a little lazy.

senses.gloss: Disapproving, in *take a dim view of*.
examples: The school takes a *dim* view of cheating.
My parents took a *dim* view of my new boyfriend.

contrast: Double the *d*: *redder*, *reddest*. Red hair is *red* (рыжий) in American English; *ginger* is mainly British and *orange hair* means dyed. In US politics *red* means Republican and *blue* means Democratic, the opposite of the old link between red and the left, so *a red state* is a conservative one. *In the red* (в минусе) uses the noun.

senses.gloss: Having the color of blood or ripe tomatoes.
examples: She wore a *red* dress to the party.
Stop when the light turns *red*.
These tomatoes are *redder* than the ones from the store.

senses.gloss: Of hair or fur: orange-brown.
examples: Both of their kids have *red* hair.
A *red* fox ran across the road.

senses.gloss: Of the face or eyes: red because of anger, embarrassment, crying or tiredness.
examples: He turned *red* when she mentioned his name.
Her eyes were *red* from crying.
His face got *redder* and *redder*.

senses.gloss: US politics: voting mostly for the Republican Party.
examples: Wyoming is one of the *reddest* states in the country.
The rural counties are deep *red*.

position: both — but *happy* in greetings (*Happy birthday*) and meaning lucky (*a happy accident*) only before a noun
takes: *with* or *about* + noun (satisfied); *for* + person (glad for their sake); *to*-infinitive (glad, willing); *that*-clause
contrast: *y* becomes *i*: *happier*, *happiest*, *happily*, *happiness*; *more happy* is rare. *Happy to* often means willing (*I'm happy to help* = охотно помогу), not счастлив. *Happy for you* = рад за тебя; *happy with* = доволен (*I'm happy with my new car*). Russian счастливый meaning lucky (*счастливый билет*) is *lucky*, not *happy*.

senses.gloss: Feeling pleasure, joy or contentment.
examples: The kids looked so *happy* on Christmas morning.
We're very *happy* together.
I've never been *happier*.

senses.gloss: Satisfied with something.
examples: Are you *happy* with the service?
My boss wasn't *happy* about the delay.

senses.gloss: Pleased about something, or willing to do something.
examples: I'd be *happy* to show you around.
We're *happy* that you could come.

senses.gloss: Glad because something good has happened to someone else.
examples: I'm so *happy* for you both!
We were *happy* for her when she got the job.

senses.gloss: Bringing or showing happiness.
examples: The movie has a *happy* ending.
That was the *happiest* day of my life.

senses.gloss: Used in good wishes for a holiday or special day.
examples: *Happy* birthday, Mom!
*Happy* holidays from all of us.

senses.gloss: Lucky and fortunate.
examples: Meeting her there was a *happy* accident.
By a *happy* coincidence, we were on the same flight.

contrast: *y* becomes *i*: *funnier*, *funniest*. *Funny* is not *fun*: *funny* makes you laugh (смешной) or is strange (странный), while *fun* means enjoyable (весёлый, *a fun party*). *The trip was funny* means something made you laugh, not that you had a good time. Because *funny* can also mean odd, Americans sometimes ask *funny ha-ha or funny weird?*

senses.gloss: Making you laugh.
examples: He told a really *funny* story about his first job.
She's the *funniest* person I know.
The sequel is even *funnier* than the original.

senses.gloss: Strange or surprising.
examples: The car is making a *funny* noise.
That's *funny*. I'm sure I left my keys on the table.
It's *funny* how things work out.

senses.gloss: Informal: slightly ill, or not working normally.
examples: I feel a little *funny*, so I think I'll sit down.
My knee has been *funny* since I fell.

senses.gloss: Informal: dishonest or suspicious.
examples: Don't try anything *funny*.
The auditors noticed something *funny* in the accounts.

position: both — but *heavy* meaning doing a lot (*a heavy smoker*) only before a noun
contrast: *y* becomes *i*: *heavier*, *heaviest*. Russian сильный with rain, snow, traffic, drinking or smoking is *heavy* in English: *heavy rain*, *heavy traffic*, *a heavy smoker*, never *strong rain* or *big traffic*. About a person, *heavy* is a polite word for fat. *Heavy cream* is the American name for whipping cream (жирные сливки).

senses.gloss: Weighing a lot; hard to lift or move.
examples: This suitcase is too *heavy* to carry up the stairs.
Gold is *heavier* than silver.
Jupiter is the *heaviest* planet.

senses.gloss: Of a person: large and fat.
examples: He was a *heavy* man with a gray beard.
She got *heavier* after she quit smoking.

senses.gloss: Greater in amount or force than usual.
examples: *Heavy* rain is expected tonight.
Traffic on I-95 was *heavy* this morning.
The storm caused *heavy* damage.

senses.gloss: Doing something a lot.
examples: My uncle was a *heavy* smoker.
He's a *heavy* user of social media.

senses.gloss: Serious, sad or hard to deal with.
examples: The movie is pretty *heavy* for a Friday night.
She left with a *heavy* heart.
Things got *heavy* when we started talking about money.

senses.gloss: Thick, strong or dense.
examples: Bring a *heavy* coat, because it's cold up there.
Whip the *heavy* cream until it forms peaks.

senses.gloss: Of food: rich and hard to digest.
examples: I had a *heavy* lunch and now I'm sleepy.
The sauce is too *heavy* for summer.

senses.gloss: Of air or weather: warm, humid and unpleasant.
examples: The air was hot and *heavy* before the storm.
It feels *heavier* today, like it's going to rain.

senses.gloss: Full of or loaded with something.
examples: The trees were *heavy* with apples.
Her voice was *heavy* with sarcasm.

senses.gloss: Slow, loud or needing a lot of effort.
examples: We heard *heavy* footsteps on the stairs.
My legs felt *heavy* after the run.

contrast: *y* becomes *i*: *lazier*, *laziest*, *lazily*. About a person, *lazy* is a criticism (ленивый); about an afternoon or a river it is pleasant: slow and relaxed (неторопливый). *Lazy* work or thinking shows too little effort (халтурный), which is harsher than *careless*.

senses.gloss: Not willing to work or make an effort.
examples: He's too *lazy* to cook, so he orders pizza.
My brother is even *lazier* than I am.
Don't be so *lazy*. Get up and help.

senses.gloss: Slow and relaxed, with little activity.
examples: We spent a *lazy* Sunday afternoon at the lake.
The river moved in *lazy* curves through the valley.

senses.gloss: Showing too little care, effort or thought.
examples: That's just *lazy* writing.
Blaming the players is the *laziest* explanation.

position: both — but *pretty* in *a pretty penny* only before a noun
contrast: *y* becomes *i*: *prettier*, *prettiest*. The adverb *pretty* (довольно) is more common in American speech than the adjective and has nothing to do with beauty: *pretty ugly* = довольно уродливый. The adjective is weaker than *beautiful* and is used for women, children and things; for a man, say *handsome* or *good-looking*.

senses.gloss: Of a woman, girl or child: attractive in a delicate way.
examples: She was a *pretty* girl with long curly hair.
Your daughter gets *prettier* every year.

senses.gloss: Of a thing or place: pleasant to look at or listen to.
examples: They live in a *pretty* little town in Vermont.
What a *pretty* dress!
It's the *prettiest* beach on the island.

senses.gloss: Informal, in fixed phrases: large, in *a pretty penny*, or unpleasant, in *not a pretty sight*.
examples: That house must have cost a *pretty* penny.
After the storm, the yard was not a *pretty* sight.

position: both — but *tidy* meaning large (*a tidy sum*) only before a noun
contrast: *y* becomes *i*: *tidier*, *tidiest*. *Tidy* sounds a little British; Americans more often call a room *neat* or *clean*, and *clean up* or *straighten up* a room more often than they *tidy it up*. *A tidy sum* has nothing to do with order: it means a lot of money (кругленькая сумма).

senses.gloss: Of a place or thing: neat and in order.
examples: Her desk is always *tidy*.
The kitchen looks *tidier* than it did this morning.
They keep a *tidy* little garden.

senses.gloss: Of a person: liking to keep things neat.
examples: My roommate is much *tidier* than I am.
He's a *tidy* dresser.

senses.gloss: Neat, simple and well organized.
examples: The show wraps everything up in a *tidy* ending.
Real life is rarely that *tidy*.

senses.gloss: Informal, of money: fairly large.
examples: They sold the house for a *tidy* profit.
She earns a *tidy* sum as a consultant.

takes: *at* or *with* + person; *about* or *over* + thing or situation; *that*-clause; *to*-infinitive (*angry to hear*)
contrast: *y* becomes *i*: *angrier*, *angriest*; *more angry* is also heard. The preposition depends on the target: *angry at* or *with* someone, *angry about* or *over* something, never *angry on*. Russian злой about a person's or a dog's nature is *mean* or *vicious*, not *angry*: *angry* is a feeling at a given moment. *Mad* is the everyday American word (*She's mad at me*).

senses.gloss: Feeling or showing strong annoyance.
examples: She was *angry* with me for forgetting her birthday.
An *angry* crowd gathered outside city hall.
Voters are *angrier* about prices than about crime.

senses.gloss: Of a wound or rash: red, swollen and painful.
examples: He had an *angry* red scar on his arm.
The bite turned into an *angry* rash.

senses.gloss: Of the sky or sea: dark and stormy.
examples: *Angry* clouds rolled in from the west.
The sea looked gray and *angry*.

contrast: *y* becomes *i*: *hungrier*, *hungriest*. *I'm hungry* = я голоден, хочу есть. *Very hungry* is fine, but *starving* is already extreme: *I'm starving*, not *very starving*. In *hungry for success*, *hungry* means eager (жаждущий), and a *hungry* player is an ambitious one. *The hungry* means people who do not have enough food.

senses.gloss: Wanting or needing food.
examples: I'm *hungry*. Let's get something to eat.
The *hungry* kids ate everything on the table.
I was *hungrier* than I thought.

senses.gloss: Not having enough food to live on, over a long time.
examples: The food bank feeds *hungry* families across the city.
Millions of children still go to bed *hungry*.

senses.gloss: Having a strong wish for something; eager and ambitious.
examples: The team is *hungry* for a championship.
They hired a young, *hungry* sales team.
After losing last year, she's *hungrier* than ever.

contrast: *y* becomes *i*: *noisier*, *noisiest*. *Loud* describes the sound itself (громкий: *loud music*, *a loud voice*); *noisy* describes the people, machines or places that make too much noise (*noisy neighbors*, *a noisy bar*). *Noisy music* is wrong; say *loud music*.

senses.gloss: Making a lot of noise, or full of noise.
examples: Our upstairs neighbors are really *noisy*.
We couldn't talk in such a *noisy* restaurant.
The new dishwasher is *noisier* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Loudly demanding attention or complaining.
examples: A small but *noisy* group opposed the plan.
The protests got *noisier* after the vote.

senses.gloss: Of data or a signal: mixed with unwanted random information.
examples: The data from the sensor was too *noisy* to use.
The recording is *noisy*, but you can hear the words.

position: both — but *dirty* about a look (*a dirty look*) or a color (*dirty blond*) only before a noun
contrast: *y* becomes *i*: *dirtier*, *dirtiest*. Russian грязный covers more than *dirty*: a road covered in mud is *muddy*, and very dirty is *filthy*. *A dirty look* is an angry glance (злой взгляд), not an unwashed face; *dirty blond* is a dull, darker blond. *Dirty* is also a verb (*Don't dirty the carpet*).

senses.gloss: Not clean.
examples: Put your *dirty* clothes in the basket.
The kitchen floor is *dirty* again.
This is the *dirtiest* car I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Dishonest, unfair or illegal.
examples: The campaign used *dirty* tricks to win.
He was accused of being a *dirty* cop.
Politics is getting *dirtier* every year.

senses.gloss: About sex in a rude way.
examples: He told a *dirty* joke at dinner.
You have a *dirty* mind!

senses.gloss: Unpleasant or hard, and often not respected.
examples: She let other people do the *dirty* work.
Mining is hard, *dirty* work.

senses.gloss: Angry or disapproving, in *a dirty look*.
examples: She gave me a *dirty* look when I laughed.
Why are you giving me *dirty* looks?

senses.gloss: Of a color: dull and not bright.
examples: He has *dirty* blond hair.
The walls were a *dirty* white.

senses.gloss: Causing a lot of pollution.
examples: Coal is one of the *dirtiest* sources of energy.
The old plant still burns *dirty* fuel.

contrast: The comparative changes *y* to *i*: *drier*, *driest*. *Dryer* is also accepted as the comparative, but in American English *dryer* usually means the machine (сушилка: *a clothes dryer*, *a hair dryer*). The adverb keeps the *y*: *dryly*. Dry wine is сухое, but *dry humor* is deadpan (невозмутимый), not cold. *A dry county* bans the sale of alcohol.

senses.gloss: Without water or other liquid; not wet.
examples: Keep the matches in a *dry* place.
Are the towels *dry* yet?
My mouth was *dry* and my hands were shaking.

senses.gloss: Of weather or a place: with little or no rain.
examples: Arizona has a hot, *dry* climate.
This has been the *driest* summer on record.
It's *drier* inland than on the coast.

senses.gloss: Of skin or hair: without enough natural oil.
examples: My skin gets really *dry* in winter.
This shampoo is for *dry* hair.

senses.gloss: Of food: without enough moisture.
examples: The chicken was overcooked and *dry*.
This cake is *drier* than last time.

senses.gloss: Of wine: not sweet.
examples: I'd like a glass of *dry* white wine.
Do you prefer *dry* or sweet?

senses.gloss: Of humor: said seriously, as if not meant to be funny.
examples: He has a very *dry* sense of humor.
Her *dry* comments had the whole room laughing.

senses.gloss: Boring and without interest.
examples: The lecture was long and *dry*.
The textbook is *drier* than dust.

senses.gloss: Without alcohol: where alcohol is not sold, or of a person who no longer drinks.
examples: It's a *dry* county, so you can't buy beer here.
The wedding was completely *dry*.
He's been *dry* for two years.

position: both — but *shy of* meaning a little less than (*just shy of 40*) only after a verb or an amount (*two points shy*)
takes: *about* or *of* + noun or *-ing* (unwilling); *of* + an amount, time or age (a little less than)
contrast: Unlike *dry*, the *y* usually stays: *shyer*, *shyest* are the common American forms, though dictionaries also give *shier*, *shiest*; *shyly* and *shyness* keep it too. Russian стесняться is often *be shy*, but feeling bad about something you did is *ashamed* or *embarrassed*. *Just shy of* is American and means a little less than (чуть меньше, не хватает до): *just shy of $1 million*.

senses.gloss: Nervous and uncomfortable with other people, especially new ones.
examples: He was a *shy* kid who hardly talked in class.
Don't be *shy*. Come say hi.
She's *shyer* than her older sister.

senses.gloss: Of an animal: easily frightened and staying away from people.
examples: Deer are *shy* animals.
The *shyest* birds stay deep in the woods.

senses.gloss: Unwilling or nervous about doing something.
examples: Don't be *shy* about asking for help.
He's never been *shy* of giving his opinion.

senses.gloss: Chiefly US: a little less than a certain amount, time or age.
examples: She died just *shy* of her 100th birthday.
The team finished two points *shy* of the record.

contrast: Like *shy*, the *y* usually stays: *slyer*, *slyest*, *slyly*, though *slier* and *sliest* also appear. *Sly* can be bad (хитрый, коварный: *a sly liar*) or friendly (лукавый: *a sly smile*); *cunning* is about deceiving, and *clever* is usually praise. *On the sly* (тайком) uses *sly* as a noun.

senses.gloss: Clever at tricking people and hiding what you intend.
examples: He's a *sly* old fox, so don't trust him.
It was a *sly* move to get us to pay.
The *slyest* players never look like they're cheating.

senses.gloss: Showing that you know a secret or are making a quiet joke.
examples: She gave me a *sly* smile.
The show is full of *sly* jokes about Hollywood.

position: both — but *simple* meaning nothing more than (*the simple truth*) only before a noun
contrast: Drop the *e* and add *-r*: *simpler*, *simplest*. *More simple* is possible but less common, and *simplier* does not exist. The adverb is *simply* (просто), which also means just: *I simply forgot*. For a task, *easy* is often more natural; *simple* suits things with few parts or steps. Calling a person *simple* can mean not intelligent, so be careful.

senses.gloss: Easy to understand or do.
examples: The instructions are *simple*.
There's a *simpler* way to do this.
It's not as *simple* as it sounds.

senses.gloss: Plain, without extra decoration or detail.
examples: She wore a *simple* black dress.
We had a *simple* meal of bread and soup.
The *simplest* designs are often the best.

senses.gloss: Nothing more than; used for emphasis.
examples: The *simple* truth is that we can't afford it.
He was late for the *simple* reason that he overslept.

senses.gloss: Made of one part or only a few parts; not complex in structure.
examples: Bacteria are *simple* organisms.
'I left' is a *simple* sentence.

senses.gloss: Ordinary; not rich or important.
examples: My grandparents were *simple* farmers.
He enjoyed the *simple* pleasures of life.

senses.gloss: Old-fashioned and offensive: not very intelligent.
examples: The neighbors thought he was a little *simple*.
Don't talk to me like I'm *simple*.

takes: *with* + person or thing (careful not to hurt)
contrast: Drop the *e* and add *-r*: *gentler*, *gentlest*, not *gentlier*; the adverb is *gently*. Russian нежный is often *tender*, *soft* or *delicate* rather than *gentle*: *gentle* is about kindness and lack of force. Russian мягкий about climate is *mild*, not *gentle*.

senses.gloss: Kind, calm and careful not to hurt anyone.
examples: He's a big man, but very *gentle*.
Be *gentle* with the baby.
She has a *gentle* voice.

senses.gloss: Not strong or violent.
examples: A *gentle* breeze came off the lake.
Give the door a *gentle* push.
The rain was *gentler* by morning.

senses.gloss: Of a slope or curve: not steep or sharp.
examples: The trail climbs a *gentle* slope.
The road makes a *gentle* curve to the left.

senses.gloss: Mild and not harmful to the body.
examples: Use a *gentle* soap for sensitive skin.
Swimming is one of the *gentlest* forms of exercise.

senses.gloss: Of a hint or criticism: tactful and polite.
examples: This is just a *gentle* reminder that rent is due.
She gave him a *gentle* hint that it was time to leave.

position: both — but *humble* about origins, things and politeness (*humble beginnings*, *my humble apologies*) mostly before a noun
contrast: Drop the *e* and add *-r*: *humbler*, *humblest*, though *more humble* is at least as common in speech. Russian скромный about a price, salary or success is *modest* (*a modest salary*, *modest about her success*), not *humble*; *humble* is about not thinking yourself more important than others. *Humbled* and *humbling* come from the verb *humble*.

senses.gloss: Not proud; not thinking you are better than others.
examples: Despite her fame, she stayed *humble*.
He's one of the *humblest* people I've ever met.
Losing made him a *humbler* man.

senses.gloss: Low in social position or money.
examples: He rose from *humble* beginnings to become a senator.
They grew up in a *humble* house in rural Ohio.

senses.gloss: Simple and ordinary, not special or important.
examples: The *humble* potato has fed millions of people.
Jeans started out as *humble* work clothes.

senses.gloss: Used to show respect or politeness when speaking of yourself.
examples: Please accept my *humble* apology.
In my *humble* opinion, the movie was too long.

position: both — but *noble* in chemistry (*noble gases*) only before a noun
contrast: Drop the *e* and add *-r*: *nobler*, *noblest*, the forms learners forget, though *more noble* is also correct. Russian благородный about a person's character is *noble*, but about manners or looks it is often *refined* or *elegant*. *A noble* is also a noun (дворянин).

senses.gloss: Morally good, brave or unselfish.
examples: Teaching is a *noble* profession.
It was a *noble* thing to do.
Is there a *nobler* cause than feeding the hungry?

senses.gloss: Belonging to a family of high social rank.
examples: She was born into a *noble* family in Spain.
His ancestors were of *noble* birth.

senses.gloss: Impressive in size or appearance.
examples: The lion is a *noble* animal.
The *noblest* building on campus is the old library.

senses.gloss: Chemistry: not reacting easily with other substances.
examples: Helium and neon are *noble* gases.
Gold and platinum are *noble* metals.

contrast: The *b* is silent: /ˈsʌtəl/. Drop the *e* and add *-r*: *subtler*, *subtlest*; *more subtle* is also common. The adverb is *subtly*, with no *e*. Russian тонкий is *subtle* only for small, clever or delicate things (*a subtle difference*, *subtle humor*); a thin slice or wire is *thin*. *Not very subtle* about a person means obvious or tactless.

senses.gloss: Small and not obvious, but important.
examples: There's a *subtle* difference between the two words.
The changes were *subtle* but real.
The *subtlest* signs of illness are the easiest to miss.

senses.gloss: Of a taste, smell or color: delicate and pleasant, not strong.
examples: The wine has a *subtle* taste of cherry.
She wore a *subtle* shade of lipstick.

senses.gloss: Clever and indirect; not stated openly.
examples: He dropped a *subtle* hint about his birthday.
You could try a *subtler* approach.
My mom isn't very *subtle* when she wants grandchildren.

senses.gloss: Able to notice and understand small differences.
examples: She has a *subtle* mind and a sharp eye.
It takes a *subtle* reader to catch the irony.

contrast: It has two syllables, but it takes *-er*: *narrower*, *narrowest*; *more narrow* is possible but less common. Russian узкий about clothes is usually *tight* or *slim* (*tight jeans*, *skinny jeans*), not *narrow*. *A narrow win* and *a narrow escape* mean something only just happened (едва, с трудом).

senses.gloss: Small in width compared with length.
examples: The streets in the old town are *narrow* and steep.
The river gets *narrower* farther north.
We squeezed through a *narrow* opening.

senses.gloss: Limited in range, ideas or experience.
examples: The law uses a very *narrow* definition of 'family.'
He has pretty *narrow* views about women.

senses.gloss: Only just achieved; by a small amount.
examples: She won by a *narrow* margin.
It was the *narrowest* victory in the state's history.
We had a *narrow* escape when the tree fell.

contrast: It has two syllables, but it takes *-er*: *shallower*, *shallowest*. Russian мелкий meaning small is not *shallow*: мелкие деньги is *change*, мелкий шрифт is *small print*, мелкий дождь is *drizzle*. About people and ideas, *shallow* is a criticism (поверхностный, пустой).

senses.gloss: Not deep; with only a short distance from top to bottom.
examples: The kids played in the *shallow* end of the pool.
The creek is *shallow* enough to walk across.
The water gets *shallower* near the shore.

senses.gloss: Not serious; not caring about or understanding important things.
examples: He's handsome but kind of *shallow*.
The characters in the movie are *shallow*.
It was the *shallowest* conversation I've had all year.

senses.gloss: Of breathing: taking in only a little air.
examples: His breathing was fast and *shallow*.
She took a few *shallow* breaths.

takes: *with* + noun (*clever with money*, *with her hands*); *at* + noun or *-ing*; *of* + person + *to*-infinitive (*clever of you to*)
contrast: It has two syllables, but it takes *-er*: *cleverer*, *cleverest*; Americans also say *more clever*. In American English *smart* is the everyday word for умный; *clever* often means ingenious or a little cunning (хитроумный), so *a clever lawyer* is not always praise. *Clever of you* judges an action: *That was clever of you*.

senses.gloss: Quick to learn and understand.
examples: She's a *clever* kid who taught herself to read.
Crows are *cleverer* than most people think.

senses.gloss: Skillful at doing something.
examples: He's very *clever* with his hands.
She's *clever* at getting people to talk.

senses.gloss: Of an idea, plan or thing: showing intelligence and original thinking.
examples: What a *clever* idea!
It was the *cleverest* ad of the Super Bowl.
It was *clever* of you to bring an extra charger.

senses.gloss: Quick with words in a way that is not sincere or respectful.
examples: Don't get *clever* with me, young man.
His answers were *clever* but didn't really say anything.

contrast: Do not confuse *quiet* /ˈkwaɪət/ (two syllables, тихий) with *quite* /kwaɪt/ (one syllable, довольно): the *e* and the *t* swap places. Though it has two syllables, *quiet* takes *-er*: *quieter*, *quietest*. *Be quiet!* means stop talking (замолчи), and *a quiet day* at work is one with little to do, not only one without noise.

senses.gloss: Making little or no noise.
examples: The house was *quiet* after the kids left.
Could you be a little *quieter*? The baby's asleep.
She spoke in a *quiet* voice.

senses.gloss: Calm and peaceful, with little activity.
examples: We live on a *quiet* street.
It's been a *quiet* week at the office.
Mondays are usually our *quietest* day.

senses.gloss: Of a person: not talking much.
examples: He's a *quiet* guy, but he's funny once you know him.
You're very *quiet* tonight. Is something wrong?

senses.gloss: Not showy or loud, but still felt.
examples: She has a *quiet* confidence.
The hotel has a *quiet* elegance.

senses.gloss: Private and not told to other people.
examples: Keep it *quiet* until we tell the family.
The company kept the layoffs *quiet* for weeks.

contrast: Drop the *e* and add *-r*: *larger*, *largest*. *Large* is more formal than *big* and is the normal word with *amount*, *number*, *quantity*, *scale* and sizes (*a large amount*, *a large coffee*). It cannot mean important, older or popular: *a big mistake*, *my big brother*, never *a large mistake* or *my large brother*. *At large* is a set phrase: *still at large* = на свободе, *the public at large* = в целом. The adverb *largely* means mostly, not on a large scale.

senses.gloss: Big in size, number or amount.
examples: They need a *larger* apartment now that the baby's here.
A *large* number of people signed the petition.
Alaska is the *largest* state.

senses.gloss: Of a size of clothes, food or drink: bigger than medium.
examples: Can I get a *large* coffee?
The *large* T-shirts sold out first.

senses.gloss: Of a person: tall and heavy; a polite word.
examples: He was a *large* man with a deep voice.
The dress looks good on *larger* women too.

senses.gloss: Wide in scope; general.
examples: This case raises *larger* questions about free speech.
We need to look at the *larger* picture.

position: both — and after a measurement: *six feet wide*
contrast: Drop the *e* and add *-r*: *wider*, *widest*. Russian широкий for shoulders or a general idea is usually *broad*: *broad shoulders*, *in broad terms*. In *wide open* and *wide awake*, *wide* is an adverb, and *widely* means by many people (*widely known*). The suffix *-wide* means across a whole area (*nationwide*).

senses.gloss: Measuring a large distance from side to side.
examples: The road is *wide* enough for two trucks.
They sat on a *wide* front porch.
The Mississippi is *wider* than I expected.

senses.gloss: Measuring a given distance from side to side.
examples: The river is about 200 yards *wide* here.
How *wide* is the doorway?

senses.gloss: Including many different things or people.
examples: The store sells a *wide* range of products.
The show appeals to a *wide* audience.
This school offers the *widest* choice of classes in the district.

senses.gloss: Large in degree or difference.
examples: There is a *wide* gap between rich and poor.
She won by a *wide* margin.

senses.gloss: Of eyes: fully open.
examples: The children watched with *wide* eyes.
His eyes went *wide* with surprise.

senses.gloss: Of a shot or throw: missing the target to one side.
examples: The kick was *wide* to the right.
His first shot was just *wide* of the goal.

position: both — but *true* meaning real (*a true friend*) mostly before a noun
takes: *to* + noun (loyal, faithful: *true to his word*); *of* or *for* + noun (applies to); *that*-clause (*It's true that*)
contrast: Drop the *e* and add *-r*: *truer*, *truest*, but the adverb *truly* loses the *e* completely (not *truely*). Russian верно! or правда! as an answer is *That's true* or *That's right*; about a person, say *You're right*, never *You're true*. *True of* or *true for* means applies to (справедливо для): *The same is true of cats*.

senses.gloss: Based on facts; not false.
examples: Is it *true* that you're moving to Denver?
The movie is based on a *true* story.
Nothing could be *truer*.

senses.gloss: Real and genuine.
examples: She's a *true* friend.
Nobody knew his *true* feelings.
Their dream finally came *true*.

senses.gloss: Loyal and faithful.
examples: He stayed *true* to his word.
The band has remained *true* to its roots.
Be *true* to yourself.

senses.gloss: Accurate; exactly matching the real thing.
examples: The painting is *true* to life.
A compass doesn't point to *true* north.

senses.gloss: Applying to someone or something.
examples: The same is *true* of most big cities.
That's especially *true* for older workers.
